Spending 20-40 unattended turns iterating on them is a bad fit whoever benefits, and the backlog being convenient is not a reason. Greenfield replaces this phase: the operator writes a spec and a planner decomposes it.

OPERATOR'S CALL (CLOSED-LOOP.md 11.2). Instinct: yes where the plan was written in the requester's own thread and they saw it; no where an agent invented it unilaterally. That is a judgement about users, not about code.

DROPPED: MOOT, not answered. Greenfield removes the situation: the loop no longer touches sites anyone asked for, so there is no case in which it might re-publish one. Deleting the question beats deciding it. Recorded rather than erased because the reasoning is what makes the deletion legible.

Two reasons, and the second is the larger one. (1) The lab factory's sites are strangers' requests — their projects. An unattended wave of turns is a bad fit for work someone else asked for. (2) THE JUDGE. CLOSED-LOOP 3 is the real blocker: nothing in this repo scores whether a thing is good. On a requested website, better can only be scored by a model against a rubric — the least trustworthy instrument available, needing the most calibration, on work we can least afford to get wrong. Choosing our own target lets us choose a domain with an ORACLE: a score that is not a model's opinion. That converts the hardest unbuilt component into a cheap one. THE COST, stated plainly: the 542-concept pool and the 59 BRIEF.md handoffs were the abundant backlog long-horizon work needs. Greenfield starts with an empty ready queue, and the outbox gate structurally forbids an agent filling it. That is why the planner role becomes necessary rather than optional.
title: DECIDED: the loop runs on a standalone greenfield project, not on community submissions

body: Greenfield collapses the target choice and CLOSED-LOOP 11.1 into ONE decision. Criteria: an oracle (a score that is not a model's opinion); enough depth that turn 30 has real work; the coupling the estate deliberately lacks; self-contained (no third-party rights, no live data, runs in the sandbox); and able to fail visibly, or it is not an experiment. Recommendation offered and NOT taken: an interpreter and a compiler for one small language, cross-checked by differential testing on generated programs. Operator is describing a different target — pressure-test it against the criteria above and say where it is weak BEFORE committing turns.
title: Choose the greenfield target — this also settles the coupling shape

body: Does not exist. The fleet half is built (loop-work); the crew half is not. Greenfield has no inherited backlog, so something must produce one. Needs its own workflow (loop-plan.yml), and it must NOT be the same agent that implements.
title: The planner role: a decomposer that turns a spec into an epic tree

body: Today loop-apply-outbox.mjs creates every agent proposal as 'proposed', full stop. Correct and too strict for unattended greenfield: nothing would ever become ready without a human at the keyboard. The right rule is that no agent may promote a bead IT AUTHORED — checkable from the actor field the ledger already records, and exactly the crew/fleet split (designer != implementer != reviewer). This is a RELAXATION OF A SAFETY PROPERTY: do not ship it before phase 1 has run human-promoted at least once. Earn it.
title: Generalise the promotion gate from 'not its own work' to 'not a bead it authored'

body: Sources, processors, defenses and sinks summoned into the voronoi foam as Platonic cells. Stays a puzzle platformer, not a sandbox. Chosen over a compiler, a solver family and a research graph because it is the only candidate that is testable (foam already carries a constructive solvability proof), attractive (strangers click a first-person 3D puzzle; nobody visits a compiler), and deep enough that the agents will genuinely struggle.
title: foam-factorio — production inside the lattice, and the loop's target

body: A cell's face normals ARE its neighbour directions, so the constellation is the dual solid's vertices. Exact for all five solids at every aniso tested. verify() is the machine half of the judge for this mechanic: a summon either produced the solid it claimed or it did not, and that is a number.
title: The summon primitive: Platonic cells from a seed constellation

body: foam's metric is anisotropic (aniso 2.2), so the bisector normal is M*n, NOT n. Placing neighbours at unit directions times a common radius rotates every off-axis face by 22 degrees. A cube survives because axis-aligned normals are the only ones M cannot rotate — which is the worst outcome, since the cube is what anyone tries first. The wrong conclusion this invites is 'voronoi cells just aren't regular'. They are. n = 2r*Minv*u / (u^T*Minv*u). Do not re-derive this; do not trust a cube as evidence.
title: Naive seed constellations are 22 degrees wrong — and the CUBE still looks perfect

body: acos is ill-conditioned near 1: for vectors agreeing to machine precision, dot = 1-eps with eps~2e-16 and acos returns sqrt(2*eps) ~ 2e-8 rad ~ 1.2e-6 degrees. That reads as a real error and invites either 'fixing' exact geometry or widening the tolerance until the check stops catching the 22-degree bug it exists for. Use atan2(|cross|, |dot|) — accurate all the way to zero.
title: Math.acos(dot) reports 1.2e-6 degrees of noise for exact unit vectors

body: constellation() did not return its own rotate parameter, so verify() compared a yawed solid against unrotated normals and reported 36 degrees of error for a 36 degree yaw. A checker that FAILS CORRECT WORK is worse than no checker: it retires a mechanic that was fine, and the retirement looks like evidence.
title: A verifier grading against the wrong reference failed correct geometry by exactly the yaw angle

body: deploy-foam.yml triggers only on claude/voronoi-foam-interactive-keo0uy. The loop runs on its own branch, so adding foam/** to the loop's writes wakes NO new workflow — verified with the blast-radius checker. This is the right shape: a human merge is the publication step, so a human decides what strangers see. It is also a hard constraint on feedback latency, and it is why the audience ladder cannot be a per-turn gate.
title: A loop commit under foam/** deploys nothing — deploy-foam is branch-locked

body: reformPocket(pocket, point) inserts ONE seed and re-derives closure + nav. A half-inserted dodecahedron is not a dodecahedron, so a constellation must land as one transaction with a single closure-and-nav gate at the end — not 13 sequential calls, each of which can refuse. Refusal must roll the whole thing back and say which seed collided.
title: Atomic multi-insert: reformPocket for a whole constellation, all-or-nothing

body: clearanceNeeded() gives the radius that must be free, but the real test is against a pocket's existing seeds AND the indestructible hull. Make 'can I build here?' answerable BEFORE attempting, so the UI can show buildable space rather than failing on click. Needing clear ground to place a factory is the oldest rule in the genre — the constraint is the mechanic.
title: Summon legality as a decidable predicate in a real pocket

body: Which solid means what, what a recipe looks like, and how a role is marked in the render (baseSeedCount already amber-shifts planted chambers — the existing hook). Defenses are the one that may imply an adversary, which would turn the build certificate into a strategy rather than a plan. That is a much larger commitment than the other three — see FACTORIO.md 7.2.
title: Object kinds: sources, processors, defenses, sinks as cell roles

body: Sources emit rates, processors transform, sinks demand: a factory is a flow network and satisfiability is a feasibility question over a small non-negative linear system. Exact, cheap, no search, no heuristics. The MARGIN by which a recipe set is satisfiable is also a difficulty dial, the way parMin/parTarget band the walk today.
title: Production feasibility oracle — the algebra

body: Prove there exists an ordered sequence of walks and summons such that each summon is legal when attempted, the walker can reach each site GIVEN THE LATTICE AS IT STANDS, and the finished production graph meets demand. The difficulty is that the actions mutate the state space they are searched over: summoning reforms the lattice, so placing an object can open a route, close one, or strand the walker. This is a planning problem over a self-modifying graph — a real CS problem, not a content problem. This is where the turns go.
title: THE BUILD CERTIFICATE — a legal ordering over a self-modifying lattice

body: generatePocket retries maxSalt=24 seeds until a walk certificate exists. The factorio generator must retry until a PLAN exists, and that search is orders of magnitude larger. Keep the invariant that no unproven pocket is ever returned.
title: Generation searches build PLANS, not just salts

body: Par counts breaches today. It becomes a cost over breaches + summons + distance, and the puzzle band moves with it. Without this there is no difficulty oracle for factory levels and 'par in band' stops meaning anything.
title: Par and the difficulty band generalise to build cost

body: A dodecahedron is 13 seeds; ten is +130 against a base pocket of ~294, and buildComplex runs on every summon while mobile performance is a hard requirement. Rich factories and the frame budget pull against each other. Turn this from a discipline into a NUMBER the judge reads, or gate 7 does not exist.
title: Per-turn frame-budget number under N summons on mobile

Ship the A/B comparison against two HAND-MADE variants and count votes. Randomise order, record it, and check the control: if position predicts preference better than version does, the signal is noise. A negative result here ends the programme for zero model spend — which is the best kind of phase, and the reason this is P0.
title: PHASE 0 — will strangers actually vote? Ship the pairwise page against hand-made variants

title: How do strangers vote, and where is it stored?

body: OPERATOR'S CALL, and there is a KNOWN INCONSISTENCY until it is made: FACTORIO.md 5 argues the quality signal should be pairwise preference between consecutive turns' output, while .github/loop/config.json still lists signals [probes, rubric, adversarial]. The config was left alone deliberately rather than edited to match the prose — it is the live control surface and this is a design decision, not a typo. The argument for the swap: the programme's question is 'does turn 20 beat turn 19', and a pairwise A/B asks exactly that, with no rubric to write and no calibration to do. The argument against: pairwise needs traffic (see the phase 0 bead) and settles over days rather than per turn, so it cannot be a per-turn gate. Resolve this before enabling the loop, or the config and the design record disagree in public.
title: Replace the judge's 'rubric' signal with human pairwise preference?

body: Applied the Definition of Ready to the eight beads sitting in the queue an hour after authoring them. Two were PHASES pretending to be tickets (fail R1 one-turn and R2 names-its-gate). Three were class B — they BUILD gates, so they define what done means and an agent must not self-serve them. Two were human-only infrastructure with no machine gate. One was already finished and nobody had closed it. Net class-A count available to an unattended fleet: ZERO. The queue length said eight. This is the exact failure the WBS names: starved and idle look identical from outside, and a rich backlog with no schedulable work is a stalled programme reading as a healthy one. Count class A, not beads.
title: AUDIT: the ready queue held zero class-A requirements — it looked healthy and was starved

body: The chain grows by BRANCHING FACTOR, not by speed. Gain = expected successor turns per turn: below 1 it dies out, at 1 it is self-sustaining forever, above 1 it is exponential. Today gain is structurally ZERO for anything the fleet produces, because loop-apply-outbox.mjs creates every agent proposal as 'proposed' and never 'ready' — the loop drains what a human put in the queue and halts. That rule was written as a quality gate; it turns out to be the strongest regulator in the system. WBS phase 3.2, relaxing it to 'not a bead it authored', is EXACTLY the change that lifts gain off zero. It must not ship unless something else holds gain below one.
title: The promotion rule is the loop's GAIN control — it is why nothing has run away yet

body: Using the account's usage limit as the governor fails twice. Informationally: pinned at the ceiling, utilisation reads 100% whether the loop is producing or spinning, so throughput becomes a property of the limit rather than of the work — and this programme exists to measure whether the work keeps paying. Practically: the limit is shared with the operator, so a regulator whose set-point is 'all of it' collides rather than regulates. The honest version is a HEADROOM RESERVE: target a fraction, observe consumption, back off when the operator is active.
title: A rate limit is a saturation, not a regulator — and running at it destroys the measurement

body: OPERATOR'S CALL. Three mechanisms answering three different questions — may it run at all (enabled, built), how fast (a token bucket denominated in SPEND rather than turns, refilled on a clock), and until when (a lease with an expiry that the reactor refuses to dispatch past). The lease is the one that matters for unattended running: counters miscount across restarts, are ambiguous under parallelism, and — fatally — NEGLECT LETS THEM CONTINUE. A lease fails closed, and it expresses 'let it run tonight' directly, which is the actual posture. Adopting this deprecates turnsPerDay.
title: Adopt the three-mechanism regulator: enabled / spend bucket / lease?

body: claude -p --max-budget-usd bounds one turn; nothing accumulates it. Without accumulation there is no bucket, no headroom reserve and no honest cost curve — and CLOSED-LOOP 10's estimate stays the weakest number in the programme. The turn record in runs.jsonl already has a slot for it.
title: Per-turn spend accounting: make cost an observable, not an assumption

body: The chain is built; the clock is not. Hybrid: the chain may continue while tokens remain, and when the bucket empties it stops and waits for the clock to refill. Burst latency when there is budget, externally-bounded rate when there is not. Depends on CRON_GITHUB_PAT, which has never been set — workers/cron has dispatched nothing in its entire life.
title: The clock half of the hybrid: cron-driven refill so the chain cannot self-sustain

body: Supersedes lp-1dfea1's conclusion, not its analysis. That bead was right that the promotion rule sets the loop's gain, and WRONG that gain is what to bound — it conflated backlog growth with runaway spend, and those are separable. Gain above one grows the READY QUEUE, which costs bytes of JSONL and is an ASSET: long-horizon agent work is starved by too little backlog, not endangered by too much. What must be capped is WORK IN FLIGHT. Bound the worker population and the branching factor can be whatever the work demands, because throughput is set by headcount rather than backlog depth. That is how every organisation with a ticket tracker already works: nobody panics at ten thousand open tickets, they staff to a number. Seats, not gain.
title: CORRECTION: bound the POPULATION, not the gain — branching is the point

body: OPERATOR'S CALL. Three mechanisms, three questions: may it run at all (enabled, built); how hard (SEATS — a licence to occupy one concurrent turn, typed by role, allocated against demand); until when (a lease with an expiry the reactor refuses to dispatch past). Seats replace the spend-bucket proposal: a bucket regulates a rate, but seats regulate a POPULATION, which is the thing that actually needs bounding (lp-CORRECTION) and is one legible integer. A short lease with many seats is a redline sprint; a long lease with few seats is a sustained run — same two knobs, opposite settings, and neither requires guessing a turn count. Adopting this deprecates turnsPerDay and maxConcurrentWork in favour of a typed seat pool.
title: Adopt the three-mechanism regulator: enabled / SEATS / lease?

body: Fungible seats fail specifically: all-available plus demand reading 'implement' means the planner never runs and the queue starves; the other way, the backlog inflates and nothing gets built. THE RATIO BETWEEN plan AND implement SEATS IS THE PRODUCER/CONSUMER RATIO — too many of one blocks on the other, expressed as headcount rather than as hope. Seat class and model tier must be separable so implement can be Opus while judge and routine verification are not.
title: Typed seat pools and the org chart: plan / implement / review / judge

body: This is where 'demand-driven' lives. Shallow queue -> plan seats. Deep queue -> implement seats. Proposals piling up unpromoted -> review seats. Turns completing unscored -> judge seats. Repeated gate failures -> NOTHING: that is a stop condition, not a staffing problem, and an allocator that responds to failure by staffing harder spends fastest exactly when it is working worst. Backpressure is what makes an unbounded queue safe: a deep queue WITHDRAWS plan seats, so the planner cannot inflate a backlog nobody consumes.
title: The allocator: seats assigned per tick against observed demand, with backpressure

body: Replaces the total prohibition with a price. review seats are deliberately scarcer than implement seats, so the rate at which the loop can feed itself is a dial rather than a cliff. The narrow invariant that must survive: NO AGENT REVIEWS A BEAD IT AUTHORED. Class B stays never-agent-promotable — an agent that can author the gate judging it has no gate, and no seat price fixes that.
title: Promotion priced at a review seat, not prohibited

body: Today a 429 mid-turn would surface as a failed turn, and a run of them would trip repeatedGateFailures: the loop concluding it is broken when it is merely throttled, stopping for the wrong reason and leaving a misleading record. Degradation ladder in preference order: fewer seats; cheaper seats for mechanical work (gates, lint, regeneration, probes do not need the strongest model); wait for the window (the queue is durable, nothing is lost); meter to the API as an explicit spend decision. CLOSED-LOOP 8 declines exactly one option — multiple subscription accounts — and that stays declined. Nothing else here is evasion.
title: Throttled is a STATE, not a failure — release seats, hold the queue, resume

body: The seat model is also what makes the run worth watching. Show the seats and who holds them, what each is working on, what closed in the last hour, what was spawned behind it, and how the allocator is currently split. A bead retiring and three appearing behind it is the programme's heartbeat and it is currently invisible — the page renders a graph, not motion. This is the difference between a dashboard and something you leave open.
title: The seat board: make loop.mino.mobi show motion, not a snapshot

body: loop-work.yml applies its own outbox to beads.jsonl AND regenerates loop/data/graph.json AND commits both. At one seat that is fine and it is what shipped. At six seats it is a guaranteed conflict on EVERY turn, on the two files every turn touches — and the graph.json conflict is meaningless, since the file is a pure function of the ledger. Turns commit SOURCES; the integrator regenerates derived files once, after the merge. This will be the first thing that breaks when seats go above one.
title: BUG IN THE BUILD: loop-work commits the ledger and graph.json — guaranteed conflict at N>1

body: A turn that lands conflicting is DISCARDED and its bead returns to ready. No hand resolution, ever. This is affordable precisely because R1 says a requirement is one turn and R6 says a failed attempt leaves the tree as it found it — re-running 20 minutes of agent work is cheaper than a human resolving a semantic conflict, and hand resolution is the expensive resource being conserved. Corollary: repeated conflicts between the same two requirements mean R4 was WRONG about them being independent. Conflict frequency is a quality metric for the requirement factory, not just a cost.
title: Conflicts are re-work, not resolution — and that is only affordable because of the DoR

body: The audience ladder asks which of two versions is better. Turn N against turn N-1 is far below the resolution of that judgement: strangers would be voting on noise and the ladder would measure nothing. A sprint is a coherent increment — several turns integrated, gated, deployed — and that is perceptible. So sprint = merge epoch = deploy unit = judge unit, one concept doing four jobs, and the curve becomes quality against SPRINT rather than turn. Turn count stays an observable: how much was spent to move one sprint is exactly the cost-per-improvement figure the programme wants.
title: A human cannot perceive one turn's improvement — the SPRINT is the judge unit

body: OPERATOR'S CALL, and it corrects an obvious-but-wrong instinct. plant.mino.mobi would put agent-generated content inside the SSO cookie's Domain=.mino.mobi scope, inside the auth worker's wildcard origin allowlist, and inside the operator's reputation — the three reasons LAB-FACTORY 3 gives for why agent-written pages must not live there. And minomobi.com/plant/ is served by the lab worker, so a loop push would fire deploy-lab and republish forty tenant sites every sprint. A separate worker on plant.minomobi.com gives the quarantine without the blast radius (labglass/os-api precedent). Name: foam's third shiva tool is PLANT, and a plant is a factory.
title: Confirm the third surface: plant.minomobi.com, seeded from foam

body: R3 (bounded paths) and R4 (independent) already carry the mechanism as an aspiration. Enforce it and conflicts are not resolved, not merged and not detected — they are NOT CREATED. Same insight the lab factory runs on (disjoint tenant dirs never conflict), applied at finer grain because this work is not naturally disjoint. Does not cover semantic breakage; removes the bulk cheaply using a field requirements must carry anyway.
title: Path leases: the allocator refuses to co-schedule intersecting path sets

body: Collect branches; ABANDON turns still running at the deadline rather than waiting (one slow turn must not hold six — this is the step that will be got wrong first); merge conflict-free first then by priority then reject; apply all outboxes in bead-id order as ONE ledger write; regenerate derived artifacts once; preflight + blast-radius; push to the plant branch; record the sprint for the judge. Cost: one integrator run per SPRINT, not per turn — at six seats that is 17% overhead instead of 100%.
title: The integrator: one merge seat, one run per sprint, deadline-bounded

body: There is no sprint concept anywhere in the current build. Everything downstream — the barrier, the integrator, sprint-scoped judging, the curve's x-axis — needs turns to know which sprint they belong to and to branch from that sprint's base rather than from moving trunk.
title: Sprint identity: sprint id on every work order, branch name and run record

body: Git's built-in union driver takes lines from both sides, which is the correct resolution for an append-only log. Only safe when the two sides append DIFFERENT records — two turns patching the same bead would have their order decided arbitrarily. Path leasing plus one-bead-per-seat is what makes that not arise. The union driver is the net, not the plan.
title: gitattributes: *.jsonl merge=union as the net under the ledger

body: The page showed the loop's STATE and nothing about its STRUCTURE. Adds three panels rendered from config rather than hardcoded, so the page cannot drift from the governor it describes: a control diagram (operator inputs above the line, reactor, allocator, seats, graph, barrier, and the two feedback edges that make it a loop rather than a pipeline); the org chart as cards; and a 'how the gain is controlled' panel separating the three things routinely confused for one — the queue may grow freely, work in flight may not, and feeding itself is priced rather than forbidden. Seats are marked PROPOSED because nothing is wired to them yet. The refusal edge is drawn as a crossed-out line: gate failures never buy staff.
title: Publish the loop's own architecture: the machine diagram and the org chart

body: Checked immediately after a deploy, /health reported 62 beads while the committed graph.json said 63, and one edge node served an /api/graph.json with no seats field while others served it correctly. Not a bug: worker.js sets cache-control 'max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300' on those routes, which explicitly permits serving a stale copy for five further minutes while revalidating, and Cloudflare edge nodes propagate independently. Two consequences. (1) A probe run right after a deploy can report a stale count that looks exactly like a data bug — add a cache-buster query before concluding anything. (2) DO NOT build an automated gate that compares the live endpoint against the repo: it would flake for five minutes after every single sprint. Compare against the committed artifact instead — that is what gen-loop-data --check already does.
title: loop.mino.mobi /health and /api can lag the ledger by up to 5 minutes, by design

body: Found by rehearsing the chain end to end, not by reading it. loop-tick computes turns = runs.length and today = runs filtered by timestamp, and runs.jsonl is appended ONLY by loop-judge. So if the judge does not run — trigger does not fire, enabled check trips, push does not wake it, job fails — the reactor keeps reporting '0 turns so far' and dispatching FOREVER. hardStopTurns and turnsPerDay both become inert, silently, while spend continues. This is the repo's recurring failure wearing new clothes: green, healthy, and metering nothing (see workers/cron). THE METER MUST BE AT THE POINT OF SPEND: tick should append to its own turns ledger when it ISSUES a work order, not learn the count later from a downstream component that may never run. Quality measurement and budget accounting must not share a writer.
title: THE BUDGET METER IS IN THE WRONG PLACE — turns are counted from runs.jsonl, which only the JUDGE writes

body: Rehearsed with enabled flipped in the working tree: the very first bead loop-tick chose to dispatch was lp-f25c2f 'Atomic multi-insert', tagged class-b. LOOP-WBS 2.3 says class B builds a GATE — it defines what done means — and must never be fleet-dispatched, because an agent that can redefine done has no gate. The taxonomy exists in a document and in bead TAGS; the scheduler reads neither. So the loop's first autonomous act would have been the one act the design forbids. readyQueue must filter on class, and a bead with no class tag must be treated as unschedulable rather than as class A — fail closed, the same rule the blast-radius checker uses.
title: The reactor is blind to requirement class — its first-ever pick was a class-B bead

body: Rehearsed locally with a simulated agent outbox. The reactor dispatched and wrote a work order; the outbox validated and applied; three records appended; the work order and outbox were both consumed so the concurrency slot was released; the target closed with evidence and its run number; THE GATE HELD — the agent's proposal landed as 'proposed' and its finding as 'done'; and the next tick picked up the next bead. The plumbing is sound. What is not sound is what it chose to do and how it counts — see the two dead-ends filed alongside this.
title: The chain itself works: tick to work order to outbox to ledger to next tick

body: The loop's first live dispatch passed all four gates, committed the work order, and then died on four 403s: 'Permission to minormobius/agent01.git denied to github-actions[bot]'. The diagnosis is NOT a missing secret — OS_AGENT_GITHUB_TOKEN was set and the workflow's own -z guard passed. actions/checkout stores its token as an http.<host>.extraheader in the LOCAL git config, and that header takes precedence over credentials embedded in a remote URL. So 'git remote set-url origin https://x-access-token:PAT@github.com/...' was silently ignored and the push authenticated as the default Actions bot, which cannot push. Fix: persist-credentials: false on the checkout in every loop workflow. THE MISLEADING PART is that the error names the bot, which reads as 'the wrong token was configured' when in fact the right token was configured and overridden. Anything in this repo that pushes from Actions with a PAT needs this.
title: actions/checkout's persisted credentials override a remote URL's — the PAT was present and never used

body: The first real turn wrote plant/solids.mjs and plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs. They passed the containment gate. Then the commit step ran 'git add .github/loop/ loop/' — WHICH DOES NOT INCLUDE plant/ — so the files were never staged, never committed, and died with the ephemeral runner. Containment gate passed, outbox valid, agent exit 0, verdict requested, everything green, and THE ONE THING THE LOOP EXISTS TO PRODUCE WAS DISCARDED. The ledger recorded the bead as done. Fix: stage the paths from config.writes rather than a hardcoded list, so extending the loop's remit can never again forget this line. General lesson for anything that commits on behalf of an agent: the set of paths it may WRITE and the set it STAGES must come from one source, or they drift and the drift is invisible.

body: Three NUL bytes replaced the SPACES in mintId's seed template: `${bead.title}\0${bead.created}\0${bead.actor}`. Node parsed it fine (they sit inside a template literal, so they are just characters), all 44 selftests passed, lint was clean, and the loop ran. THE ONLY SIGNAL WAS git reporting 'Bin 16405 -> 18017 bytes' on a JavaScript file in a commit stat. Two lessons. (1) Passing tests do not prove a source file is well-formed — they prove it PARSES and BEHAVES, which is a weaker claim than it feels like. (2) Read the diffstat: 'Bin' on a text file is git telling you something is wrong in the only place it can. Also note what it silently changed: the id derivation moved from space-joined to NUL-joined, so ids minted before and after differ for identical inputs. Harmless here because ids are stored rather than recomputed, but a content-derived identifier whose derivation drifts is a nasty class of bug.
title: A scripted edit put NUL bytes into a .mjs source and every test still passed
